summary: Phase 2 of the myidsan productization plan ("Accountability"): an append-only security audit log, session administration, and step-up re-authentication. A new AuditLog entity/service records login success/failure/lockout/logout (with the sign-in method), MFA enroll/disable/admin-reset, user create/update/delete, directory config updates, password-reset resolution, backup export/restore, session revocation, and step-up success/failure -- the service exposes only Record and List, with no update or delete path at all, so the trail cannot be edited from inside the product. A failed sign-in is recorded with no actor id and the attempted (possibly bogus) identifier as the actor label, since the caller has no account yet; every event captures the User-Agent, which myseliasan's equivalent audit log does not. A new superadmin-only Audit log page (GET /api/audit, filterable by action/outcome/actor/target/date range) and GET /api/audit/export.csv share one filter parser so an export always matches what the screen showed; the CSV defuses spreadsheet formula injection on every attacker-influenced column (a failed-login username, a User-Agent) by quoting a leading =/+/-/@/tab/CR. Client addresses recorded anywhere in the trail go through a newly-exported domain/utils/middlewares.ClientIP/ParseTrustedProxies, extracted from the rate limiter's previously-private copy so the two features cannot disagree on which peers may declare a forwarded address -- unlike myseliasan's audit log, which trusts X-Forwarded-For unconditionally. Separately, the long-declared-but-never-written domain/entities.UserSession table is now actually populated (gained IpAddress/UserAgent/LastSeenAt) by a new ISessionService: the cache entry at sso:session:<sid> remains the authority the auth middleware checks, this table is only an index so sessions can be listed per user, and a revoke deletes the cache entry first so a bookkeeping failure can never leave a live session claiming to be dead. A self-service Sessions panel on the Profile page (GET/DELETE /api/session, POST /api/session/revoke-all, deliberately auth-only and not RBAC-matrix-gated -- the person whose laptop was stolen needs this screen unconditionally) lets a user list and end their own sessions or sign out everywhere else; a superadmin can end another account's sessions from the Users page (/api/session-admin). Disabling or deleting an account now ends its sessions too, closing a real gap where a disabled account's already-issued session kept validating against auth-only routes (/api/profile/*, /api/mfa) for up to its full 72-hour lifetime, since the cached session carries no account-status flag. Finally, a new 5-minute cache-backed step-up re-authentication marker (password, plus TOTP when a factor is enrolled) now gates the four most dangerous things a stolen 72-hour superadmin cookie could otherwise do with no further proof of identity: backup export, backup restore, resetting another user's MFA, and resolving a password-reset request. A failed step-up attempt is itself audited.
compatibility: New tables (audit_log) and newly-populated columns (user_session.ipAddress/userAgent/lastSeenAt) are additive; no existing schema is removed or restructured, and no migration step is required beyond normal bootstrap schema sync. The audit log, session list, and step-up prompt are new surfaces with no prior behavior to preserve. The only behavior change for an existing install is functional, not configurable: disabling or deleting a user account now actively ends that account's live sessions (previously it did not), and backup export/restore, MFA admin-reset, and password-reset resolve now require a fresh password (+TOTP if enrolled) re-entry within 5 minutes before they proceed -- there is no policy toggle to disable step-up, since the actions it gates are exactly the ones a stolen session cookie should not be able to reach unassisted. The audit log and session index are excluded from .idbackup export/restore by design (host-local history, like the API/runtime logs), so a restore neither carries nor erases another host's trail.
